To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single chip implementation of neuromorphic computing can achieve a 1000 times speed up with respect to biological time, while consuming 57 mW, and that learning can mitigate the adverse effects of fixed pattern and parameter noise.

(i) the BrainScaleS2 system is a viable platform for learning in spiking networks, (ii) on chip learning compensates for fixed pattern noise in analog substrates and (iii) on chip learning can be used as a mechanism for action exploration.

a single chip neuromorphic system can implement a proof of principle demonstration of learning in a spiking neural network that learns to perform an action by smooth pursuit, and that on chip learning compensates fixed pattern noise and neuronal parameter variability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and demonstration of novel neuromorphic architectures that enable the emulation of brain-like computation at accelerated speeds and with reduced power budgets.
the demonstration of advantages of neuromorphic computation in the context of learning in spiking networks.
the development of neuromorphic systems for learning, and in this work we present a proof of concept implementation of a spiking neural network that learns to solve a simple video game.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the system is a promising step towards a neuromorphic platform for real-time learning and control.
the BrainScaleS system demonstrates the advantages of neuromorphic computation, while at the same time pointing out the remaining challenges.
the BrainScaleS system is a powerful tool to study and understand how biological neural networks learn and process information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the BrainScaleS system can be used as a platform for studying the computational principles that underlie learning and adaptation in the brain, and that it is a viable alternative for studying the brain in the loop.

the BrainScaleS system is able to demonstrate that neuromorphic computation can be competitive with respect to conventional digital computing in terms of speed and energy efficiency, and that the analog substrate enables the emulation of biologically relevant neural dynamics at a speed that is sufficient to support on chip learning.
neuromorphic computing has the potential to enable efficient learning in large scale systems, and that it can provide a useful tool for studying the brain's learning mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a neuromorphic system with a mixed analog/digital substrate can be used to implement a biologically inspired learning algorithm, which is able to compensate for the imperfections of the substrate, and thereby achieve performance on par with a biological brain.
the combination of on chip learning with analog emulation of neural dynamics can be used to demonstrate the advantages of neuromorphic computing.

neuromorphic computation is a viable approach for demonstrating proof of concept demonstrations of brain inspired algorithms and architectures, which can serve as a stepping stone towards more ambitious goals.
